summary:
San Juan operates under Argentina's national framework, and no San Juan-specific source shows a deviation material enough to score separately. The province is therefore assessed at the national position.

Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, remains formally in force. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and Argentine identity documents have carried an 'X' marker since 2021. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, and the United Nations described the 2012 statute as a pioneering regional step. Activists interviewed in April 2025 told the Washington Blade that the law is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Executive action has narrowed the statute. Decree DNU 62/2025, published on 5 February 2025 under President Javier Milei, amended Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions. Decree DNU 61/2025 altered sentencing law to change how trans detainees are housed. Both decrees apply nationally and to every province, including San Juan. Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations called both measures unconstitutional, argued that abruptly suspending adolescent treatment endangers trans youth, and mounted a judicial challenge; the outcome of that challenge is not recorded in the sources.

The government eliminated the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans public servants hired under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1 per cent of public-sector posts. Activists say the quota is no longer being implemented.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people peaked in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share. Trans activists in Buenos Aires said government policy had made the community more vulnerable and described conditions as chaotic and desperate.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is unsettled. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence of Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed on appeal in 2020, so that aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

A visitor to San Juan can expect the 2012 Gender Identity Law's recognition procedure to be available on national terms, while the under-18 restrictions of DNU 62/2025 and the prison-placement rules of DNU 61/2025 apply locally as everywhere else in Argentina.
tangentialFactors:
Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, and marks an overall deterioration against the earlier statutory position. That assessment sits alongside a statute that on its face remains among the most permissive in the world, so formal law and reported practice diverge.

The 2025 hate-crime total was described by Agencia Presentes as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, and the trend is national rather than confined to any one province. Organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins were among those reporting increased vulnerability in April 2025.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws, though no San Juan-specific anti-discrimination instrument is documented in these sources.
localsOnly:
The Trans Labor Quota Law reserves 1 per cent of Argentine public-sector posts for trans people. Activists report that the Milei government dismissed trans hires made under the quota and that it is no longer being implemented, removing an employment route that residents depend on.

The national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was eliminated, removing the principal federal body through which residents previously raised gender-identity and diversity matters administratively.

Decree DNU 61/2025 amended prison-sentencing law to change the placement of trans detainees. Residents subject to the criminal justice system in San Juan fall under that amended rule.

Legal experts and LGBT+ organisations have brought both the Article 11 amendment and the prison-placement decree before the courts, arguing they are unconstitutional; residents affected by the suspension of adolescent treatment are parties to or beneficiaries of that litigation.
